entries.meaning: From Latin Epithersēs, from Ancient Greek Ἐπιθέρσης (Epithérsēs).
entries.note: A male given name

entries.meaning: From Medieval Latin Erasmus. The EU student exchange programme is named after Erasmus of Rotterdam, and also a backronym for “European [Community] Action Scheme for the Mobility of University Students”.
entries.note: A male given name from Ancient Greek, rare in English.

entries.meaning: From Ancient Greek Ἔραστος (Érastos), from ἐραστός (erastós, “lovable”).
entries.note: A male given name from Ancient Greek of biblical derivation.

entries.meaning: Unadapted borrowing from Turkish Erdoğan.
entries.note: A male given name from Turkish.

entries.meaning: From Japanese えり.
entries.note: A female given name from Japanese.

entries.meaning: From Middle English Eric, from Old English Eoric, from Old Norse Eirríkr, Eiríkr (from ei (“always, eternal”, see aye) + ríkr (“ruler”)), or from Proto-Germanic *Aizarīkijaz (from *aizō (“honor”) + *rīkijaz (“ruler”)). Less likely from einn (“sole, alone”) + ríkr (“ruler”), from Proto-Germanic *rīks (“king”, cognate to Latin rēx and Gaulish *rīx).
entries.note: A male given name from the Germanic languages.

entries.meaning: A feminine form of Eric, ultimately from Old Norse. The name has also been associated with the flower genus.
entries.note: A female given name from the Germanic languages or Old Norse.
entries.origin: the Germanic languages or Old Norse

entries.meaning: A spelling variant of Eric, or directly borrowed from modern Swedish Erik.
entries.note: A male given name from Old Norse, variant of Eric.

entries.meaning: Spelling variant of Erica, the feminine form of Eric, or borrowed directly from modern Scandinavia, ultimately from Old Norse Eiríkr.
entries.note: A female given name from the Germanic languages or Old Norse.
entries.origin: the Germanic languages or Old Norse

entries.meaning: Anglicisation of Irish Éirinn (dative singular and dialectal nominative singular of Éire (“Ireland”)).
entries.note: A female or male given name, in use since the mid-20th century, used in honor of Ireland.

entries.meaning: A rare spelling variant of Earl.
entries.note: A male given name from English.

entries.meaning: From the Old English name reinforced by its Norman cognate, from Proto-Germanic *ermunaz (“all,whole”) + *gardaz (“enclosure”), "strong protection". Cognate with the German saint's name Irmgard.
entries.note: A female given name from Old English.

entries.meaning: Shortening.
entries.note: A diminutive of the male given name Ernest.

entries.meaning: Borrowed in the 18th century from Ernst, a medieval royal name in Germany, from Old High German ernust (“vigor, strife”), only remotely related to modern German ernst or English earnest.
entries.note: A male given name from the Germanic languages; popular in the 19th century.

entries.meaning: From Italian Ernesta. By surface analysis, Ernest + -a.
entries.note: A female given name from Italian, masculine equivalent Ernest.

entries.meaning: From Italian, Portuguese, and Spanish Ernestina. By surface analysis, Ernest + -ina. Piecewise doublet of Ernestine.
entries.note: A female given name, variant of Ernestine.

entries.meaning: From French Ernestine. By surface analysis, Ernest + -ine (feminine suffix). Piecewise doublet of Ernestina.
entries.note: A female given name from French [in turn from the Germanic languages], masculine equivalent Ernest.
entries.origin: French [in turn from the Germanic languages]

entries.meaning: From Ernest + -ie.
entries.note: A diminutive of the male given name Ernest.

entries.meaning: From the Old English personal name Ēadrǣd, which is composed of the elements ēad (“prosperity”) and rǣd (“advice, wisdom”).
entries.note: A male given name from Old English.

entries.meaning: Transferred from a rare Scottish surname derived from a place name, of unknown meaning. Later interpreted as a variant of Earl in the U.S.
entries.note: A male given name transferred from the surname, popularized by American Actor Errol Flynn.

entries.meaning: From Ancient Greek Ἕρσα (Hérsa, literally “Dew”).
entries.note: A female given name.

entries.meaning: Variant of Erin.
entries.note: A female given name.

entries.meaning: From Ancient Greek Ἡσαῦ (Hēsaû), from Biblical Hebrew עֵשָׂו (ʿēśāw).
entries.note: A male given name from Hebrew.

entries.meaning: Clipping of Esmeralda.
entries.note: A diminutive of the female given name Esmeralda.

entries.meaning: Anglicized spelling of the French Esmée or Esmé
entries.note: A female given name from French.

entries.meaning: From Spanish esmeralda (“emerald”), as first used in the novel Notre-Dame de Paris (1831) by Victor Hugo.
entries.note: A female given name from Spanish.

entries.meaning: Variant of Esmeralda.
entries.note: A female given name from Spanish.

entries.meaning: Clipping of Esmerelda or Esmeralda.
entries.note: A female given name from Spanish.

entries.meaning: Inherited from Old English Ēastseaxan (literally “East Saxons”), which stood for both Essex and the people of Essex.
entries.note: A unisex given name transferred from the place name.

entries.meaning: Diminutive + -y.
entries.note: A female given name, short for Esther or Estelle.

entries.meaning: From Esther + -ee.
entries.note: A diminutive of the female given name Esther, variant of Esti.

entries.meaning: Latinized and Italian variant of the French Estelle.
entries.note: A female given name from Latin.

entries.meaning: Borrowed from French Estelle, from Occitan estela (“star”), from Latin stēlla. Doublet of étoile, estoile, stella, and stelo. Name of a third century martyr.
entries.note: A female given name from French

entries.meaning: From Ancient Greek Ἐσθήρ (Esthḗr), from Biblical Hebrew אֶסְתֵּר (ʾestēr). Has been connected to Old Persian 𐎠𐎿𐎫𐎼 (a-s-t-r /⁠star-⁠/, “star”) (whence Middle Persian 𐭮𐭲𐭫 (stl /⁠star⁠/, “star”), 𐭮𐭲𐭠𐭫𐭪 (stʾlk /⁠stārag⁠/, “star”), Persian ستاره (sitāra /setâre, “star”)), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂stḗr (if so, a distant doublet of star); or else to Akkadian 𒀭𒈹 (Ištar, “Ishtar”) (Hebrew עִשְׁתָּר (ʿištār)).
entries.note: A female given name from Persian.

entries.meaning: Rendering of the modern (Israeli) Hebrew אֵיתָן (Etán), equivalent to the English Ethan.
entries.note: A male given name from Hebrew.

entries.meaning: Short form of names of Old English origin beginning with Ethel-, æþele (“noble”). First used in the 19th century. Cognate to the Germanic Adela and Adele.
entries.note: A female given name from Old English, popular at the turn of the 20th century.

entries.meaning: Revived from Old English Æþelbeorht, from Proto-West Germanic *Aþalaberht. Compound of Old English æþele (“noble”) + beorht (“bright”). Doublet of Albert.
entries.note: A male given name from Old English revived in the 19th century.
entries.origin: Old English revived in the 19th century

entries.meaning: Learned borrowing from Old English Æþelrǣd, Æþelred, Æðelred, from æþele (“noble”) + rǣd (“counsel, advice”).
entries.note: A male given name from Old English Æþelræd (“noble counsel, well-advised”), variant of Aethelred and Æthelred. Ethelred I, King of Wessex between 865 and his death in 871.

entries.meaning: From Old English Æþelwulf, equivalent to athel (“noble”) + wolf. Doublet of Adolf.
entries.note: A male given name.

entries.meaning: Possibly an anglicisation of Irish Eithne.
entries.note: A female given name from Irish.

entries.meaning: Corruption of Italian Ettore?
entries.note: A male given name from Italian.

entries.meaning: From Ancient Greek Εὐκλείδης (Eukleídēs).
entries.note: A male given name from Ancient Greek of mostly historical use.
entries.origin: Ancient Greek of mostly historical use

entries.meaning: From Latin Otho.
entries.note: A male given name of historical usage.

entries.meaning: From Latin Eudocia, from Ancient Greek Εὐδοκία (Eudokía), from Ancient Greek εὐδοκία (eudokía, “satisfied or satisfying one”), from εὐδοκέω (eudokéō, “to be well-pleased or well-pleasing”) + -ία (-ía, “-ia: forming adjectives”), from εὐ- (eu-, “eu-: good”) + δοκέω (dokéō, “to think, to be thought, to seem”). Doublet of Evdokia.
entries.note: A female given name from Ancient Greek.

entries.meaning: From Latin Eudoxia, from Ancient Greek Εὐδοξία (Eudoxía), from εὐδοξία (eudoxía, “the famed one, the one of good repute”), from εὐ- (eu-, “eu-: good”) + δόξα (dóxa, “opinion, judgment, honor”) + -ία (-ía, “-ia: forming adjectives”).
entries.note: A female given name from Ancient Greek.

entries.meaning: Borrowed from French Eugène, from Latin Eugenius, from Ancient Greek Εὐγένιος (Eugénios, “well born”), from εὖ (eû, “good, well”) + -γενής (-genḗs, “born a certain way”). Parallel to eugenics. Doublet of Yevgeny, Eugenius, and Owen.
entries.note: A male given name from Ancient Greek.

entries.meaning: From Ancient Greek Εὐγενία (Eugenía), feminine form of Εὐγένιος (Eugénios) ( =Eugene) "well born".
entries.note: A female given name from Ancient Greek. Variant: Eugenie.

entries.meaning: Borrowed from Latin Eugenius, from Ancient Greek Εὐγένιος (Eugénios). Doublet of Eugene and Yevgeny.
entries.note: A male given name from Latin [in turn from Ancient Greek].

entries.meaning: From Latin Euhemerus, from Ancient Greek Εὐήμερος (Euḗmeros, from εὐ- (eu-, “good-, well-”) + ἥμερος (hḗmeros, “tamed, civilized, domesticated”)).
entries.note: A transliteration of the Ancient Greek male given name Εὐήμερος (Euḗmeros).

entries.meaning: Rare non-standard spelling of Eula.
entries.note: A female given name.

entries.meaning: French from the saints' name Eulalia, from Ancient Greek "sweetly speaking".
entries.note: A female given name from Ancient Greek.

entries.meaning: From Latin Eumenēs, from Ancient Greek Εὐμένης (Euménēs)
entries.note: An unknown-gender given name from Latin or Greek, of historical usage

entries.meaning: A biblical name from Ancient Greek Εὐνίκη (Euníkē), from εὐ- (eu-, “good”) + νίκη (níkē, “victory”).
entries.note: A female given name from Ancient Greek.

entries.meaning: Name of an early Christian martyr, from Ancient Greek Εὐφημία (Euphēmía), from εὐ- (eu-, “good”) + φήμη (phḗmē, “repute”) + -ίᾱ (-íā).
entries.note: A female given name from Ancient Greek.

entries.meaning: From Euphemia + -ie.
entries.note: A diminutive of the female given name Euphemia.

entries.meaning: From Ancient Greek Εὐφροσύνη (Euphrosúnē).
entries.note: A female given name from Ancient Greek.

entries.meaning: From Latin Eurichus or Spanish Eurico, both ultimately from Gothic *𐌰𐌹𐍅𐌰𐍂𐌴𐌹𐌺𐍃 (*aiwareiks). Possible doublet of Eric and Erik.
entries.note: A male given name from Gothic.

entries.meaning: From the Ancient Greek Εὐρῑπῐ́δης (Eurīpĭ́dēs).
entries.note: A male given name from Ancient Greek, mostly representing a transliteration of the modern Greek Ευριπίδης (Evripídis).

entries.meaning: From Latin Eurydicē, from Ancient Greek Εὐρυδίκη (Eurudíkē).
entries.note: A female given name.

entries.meaning: From the Old French form of Latin Eustathius, from Ancient Greek Εὐστάθιος (Eustáthios, “ancient name, also of Christian Saint”), from Ancient Greek εὐσταθής (eustathḗs, “steadfast, stable”). Or from εὔστᾰχῠς (eústăkhŭs, “fruitful”, literally “abundant in grain”), from εὖ (eû) + στάχυς (stákhus). Doublet of Ostap.
entries.note: A male given name from Ancient Greek.

entries.meaning: From Ancient Greek Εὐθυμία (Euthumía), from εὐ- (eu-, “good”) + θυμός (thumós, “disposition”).
entries.note: A female given name from Ancient Greek, meaning "of a good disposition".

entries.meaning: Ancient Greek Εὐθῠ́φρων (Euthŭ́phrōn).
entries.note: A male given name from Ancient Greek, of historical usage.

entries.meaning: The (Vulgate) Latin Eva, from Ancient Greek Εὔα (Eúa), from Biblical Hebrew חַוָּה (ḥawwā). A Latinate variant of the English Eve.
entries.note: A female given name from Latin, ultimately from Hebrew.

entries.meaning: Borrowed from Ancient Greek Εὐάδνη (Euádnē).
entries.note: A female given name from Ancient Greek.

entries.meaning: From Eva + Lyn, or a variant of Evelyn.
entries.note: A female given name originating as a coinage.

entries.meaning: Anglicization of Welsh Ifan, ultimately from Latin Jōhannēs, variant of Iōannēs, from Koine Greek Ἰωάννης (Iōánnēs), from Hebrew יוֹחָנָן (yōḥānān, yokhanán, literally “God is gracious”). Doublet of Giovanni, Ian, Ivan, Jack, Jean, Johan, Johann, Johannes, John, Sean, Shane, Shaun, and Shawn.
entries.note: A male given name from Welsh Ifan, equivalent to English John.

entries.meaning: From Latin Euander, from Ancient Greek Εὔανδρος (Eúandros, literally “good man”).
entries.note: A male given name from Ancient Greek.

entries.meaning: An alteration of Evangeline.
entries.note: A female given name originating as a coinage.

entries.meaning: Invented by the poet Henry Wadsworth Longfellow when he began research on his epic poem Evangeline about Acadian lovers deported from French-Canada. From Ancient Greek εὐαγγέλιον (euangélion, “good news”).
entries.note: A female given name originating as a coinage.

entries.meaning: From Greek Ευανθία (Evanthía) and Latin Evanthia, from Ancient Greek Εὐανθία (Euanthía, from εὐ- (eu-, “good-, well-”) + άνθος (ánthos, “blossom”) + -ία (-ía, “-ia: forming feminine abstract nouns”)). Cognate with Euanthe.
entries.note: A female given name from Greek.

entries.meaning: From Middle English Eve, Eue, from Old English Ēua, Ēfe, from Latin Eva, from Ancient Greek Εὔα (Eúa), from Biblical Hebrew חַוָּה (ḥawwā).
entries.note: A female given name from Hebrew.

entries.meaning: From Middle English forms of the Old French female name Aveline, diminutive of the Germanic root *avi-, of uncertain meaning, possibly “desired, wished for“ (compare Latin avēre, "to wish for") or aval “strength”. By folk etymology also misunderstood as a diminutive of the feminine given name Eve, q.v. Doublet of Eileen. Also compare Ava.
entries.note: A female given name from the Germanic languages.

entries.meaning: From French Évelyne.
entries.note: A female given name from French, anglicized by Évelyne.

entries.meaning: A rare non-standard spelling of Evelyn with -lynn.
entries.note: A female given name.

entries.meaning: From Old English Eofurheard, Eoferard, from Proto-West Germanic *Eburahardu, from *ebur (“wild boar”) + *hardu (“hard, brave”). Reinforced by cognate names from Anglo-Norman and Middle Dutch.
entries.note: An English surname transferred from the given name.

entries.meaning: From Dutch Everaert or Everardt (late 16th C.), from Middle Dutch Everarde. Doublet of Everard.
entries.note: A male given name from Dutch transferred back from the surname.
entries.origin: Dutch transferred back from the surname

entries.meaning: Rare variant of Everett.
entries.note: A male given name from Old English.

entries.meaning: From Old English eofor (“wild boar”) + lēah (“woodland clearing”). Compare the Dutch toponym Everlo.
entries.note: A female given name transferred from the surname.

entries.meaning: Habitational surname, from a variant of Everleigh.
entries.note: A female given name transferred from the surname.

entries.meaning: From Old English eofor (“wild boar”) + tūn (“settlement”).
entries.note: A male given name transferred from the surname.

entries.meaning: Diminutives + -ie.
entries.note: A diminutive of the female given names Eva, Eve, Evelyn, and Evangeline.

entries.meaning: From Spanish Evita, a pet form of Eva.
entries.note: A female given name from Spanish.

entries.meaning: Diminutives + -ie.
entries.note: A diminutive of the female given names Eva, Eve, Evelyn, and Evangeline.

entries.meaning: From Scottish Gaelic Eòghan. Not related to Iwan and Evan.
entries.note: A male given name from Scottish Gaelic.

entries.meaning: From Koine Greek Ἰεζεκιήλ (Iezekiḗl), from Biblical Hebrew יְחֶזְקֵאל (Y'ḥezqēl, “God strengthens”).
entries.note: A male given name from Hebrew of biblical origin. First used by Puritans in the 17th century; rare today.

entries.meaning: Borrowed from French Élisabeth.
entries.note: A female given name from French, equivalent to English Elizabeth.

entries.meaning: Borrowed from French Élise.
entries.note: A diminutive of the female given name Élisabeth.
